clue.text: Film part backing Labour includes Penelope

parts.note: some means a part or portion of something

indicators.note: includes means one piece takes another inside it
backing means the word for labour is read from the back, right to left

parts.note: labour means toil, hard work
Penelope Keith is the English actress of The Good Life fame

explanation.surface: A movie role supporting the Labour party has found room for an actress called Penelope.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' turns the labour word round to LIOT, and 'includes' puts the actress's surname in its middle. Labour here is work, not the British political party; Penelope Keith is a British sitcom star.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is the title of Billy Wilder's 1959 comedy starring Marilyn Monroe, so it is an example of a film.

clue.text: Frank people with subtle implications

parts.note: frank means open, not hidden
ones can mean people, as in 'little ones' or 'loved ones'

explanation.surface: Outspoken folk who nevertheless deal in subtle hints.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frank' looks like a man's name but is the adjective meaning candid.
explanation.definitionFit: Overtones are secondary meanings or suggestions carried beneath what is actually said.

clue.text: Writing speech on South Africa

indicators.note: speech on signals that the abbreviation is to be pronounced rather than written

parts.note: these words are said aloud, and what is heard is the sound this part of the answer needs

explanation.surface: A piece of writing about a speech given on the subject of South Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: Say the letters S and A out loud: 'ess-ay'.
explanation.definitionFit: An essay is a short piece of prose writing on a subject, so it is a kind of writing.

clue.text: Goat takes off head of reptile

indicators.note: takes off head of means the first letter of the reptile's name is removed

parts.note: a lizard is a scaly reptile

explanation.surface: A goat beheads a lizard.
explanation.walkthrough: The IZARD is a wild goat of the Pyrenees, related to the chamois.
explanation.definitionFit: The izard is the Pyrenean chamois, a goat-like mountain animal, so it counts as a goat.

clue.text: I rent a net to play at fête

indicators.note: to play means the letters are set to work in a new order

explanation.surface: Someone hires a net for a game at the village fête.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fête' looks like the noun for a village fair, but here it is the verb meaning to treat lavishly.
explanation.definitionFit: To fête someone is to honour them with lavish hospitality, which is to entertain them.

clue.text: Court divisions

parts.note: court suggests a law court split into divisions, but read it as a tennis court and its painted side lines

explanation.surface: A note on how a court of law is divided.
explanation.definitionFit: On a tennis court the pair of parallel lines at each side, marking the doubles alleys, have this name.

clue.text: Celtic runes discovered in Omagh disaster

indicators.note: disaster means the place name is wrecked, its letters thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: Ancient Celtic inscriptions turned up during the Omagh disaster.
explanation.walkthrough: Omagh is a town in Northern Ireland, scene of a 1998 bombing; the surface makes 'discovered in' sound like a hidden word, but it is a link before an anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Ogham is the early Irish and Celtic alphabet of notched strokes, often loosely called runes.

clue.text: Global warming policy?

parts.note: read literally, a policy of warming the globe by setting land on fire, rather than a climate policy

explanation.surface: A question about what climate policy should be.
explanation.definitionFit: A military strategy of burning crops and buildings so an advancing enemy finds nothing usable is known by this name.

clue.text: Measures against newcomers by European landlords

definitions.meaning: condoms are measures taken against new arrivals, that is babies
read as letters (people who let property) from France

explanation.surface: European landlords impose rules to keep out new arrivals.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is old British slang for condoms; the second reading treats 'letters' as people who let out property.
explanation.definitionFit: Contraceptives guard against babies, the newcomers, and lessors in Paris are literally landlords of that nationality.

clue.text: Church, otherwise a football club

parts.note: else means otherwise, as in 'or else'

explanation.surface: Either a church or else a football club.
explanation.walkthrough: Chelsea is a London football club.
explanation.definitionFit: Chelsea FC is a Premier League football club based in west London, so the answer is an example of a club.

clue.text: One of the care providers?

parts.note: a school is in charge of children during the day, and the words 'the care' happen to provide exactly the right letters

explanation.surface: A question about who works in the caring professions.
explanation.walkthrough: A schoolteacher acts in place of a parent, so is a provider of care; the letters of 'the care' also rearrange to the answer, a bonus.
explanation.definitionFit: A schoolteacher has pupils in their charge, so they are among those looking after children.

clue.text: Grahame's irritable character

parts.note: Kenneth Grahame wrote The Wind in the Willows, where the Water Rat is known by a nickname that also means bad-tempered

explanation.surface: A bad-tempered figure from a Kenneth Grahame book.
explanation.walkthrough: Kenneth Grahame's The Wind in the Willows features Rat, called by this nickname; the word also means irritable.
explanation.definitionFit: The Water Rat in The Wind in the Willows goes by this pet name, which is also slang for tetchy or cross.

clue.text: Metal found in mud deposit round Russian river

indicators.note: round means the jumbled letters go round the river's name
deposit means the letters are set down in a fresh arrangement

parts.note: the Ural is a river flowing through Russia into the Caspian

explanation.surface: A metal has turned up in a mud deposit near a river in Russia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'deposit' rearranges the two short words into DUMIN, and 'round' wraps that around the river, splitting it after the D. Duralumin is the alloy, not a natural mineral.
explanation.definitionFit: Duralumin is a strong, light aluminium alloy used in aircraft, so it is a metal.

clue.text: Medieval cup in auction fetching less than a pound

indicators.note: fetching here means bringing in or holding, so the words that follow contain the answer

explanation.surface: An old goblet goes under the hammer and sells for pennies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in auction fetching' reads as a sale price, but 'fetching' signals the letters held in 'less tHAN A Pound'; 'in auction' is scene-setting.
explanation.definitionFit: A hanap is an ornate medieval drinking goblet, often with a lid, so it is a cup from the Middle Ages.

clue.text: Bush's problem of failed goal in Caribbean gulf

indicators.note: in means the jumbled letters sit inside the name of the gulf

parts.note: the Gulf of Paria lies between Trinidad and Venezuela

indicators.note: failed means the word goal is broken up and its letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A failed goal somewhere in the Caribbean was a problem for President Bush.
explanation.walkthrough: 'failed' rearranges the football word into ALOG. George W. Bush was famous for verbal slips, and the Gulf of Paria lies off Trinidad.
explanation.definitionFit: Paralogia is a speech disorder producing illogical or garbled statements, a joke at the expense of George W. Bush's mangled sayings.

clue.text: What fanatics do to get support where it all comes out

parts.note: a bra is a supporting undergarment
from the saying 'it'll all come out in the wash'

explanation.surface: A question of what zealots do to win backing in a laundry.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'it will all come out in the wash' supplies IN WASH.
explanation.definitionFit: Fanatics indoctrinate others, forcing their beliefs on them until they hold no other views.

clue.text: Old Nick

parts.note: looks like a name for the Devil, but nick is British slang for a prison, so an old prison

explanation.surface: A nickname for the Devil.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang a nick is a prison or police station; Bridewell was a London house of correction whose name became a general word for a jail.
explanation.definitionFit: A bridewell was an old-fashioned jail, named after the London prison near St Bride's Well.

clue.text: A vehicle India designed for a mite

parts.note: a car is a road vehicle

indicators.note: designed means the country's name is reworked into a new shape

explanation.surface: An Indian-built car intended for a tiny buyer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'designed' makes IDIAN from INDIA. 'a mite' looks like 'a little', but is the creature.
explanation.definitionFit: Acaridians are members of the order of arachnids that includes mites and ticks, so one is a mite.

clue.text: No one returns from the wilderness — it may mean a court martial

definitions.text: it may mean a court martial

parts.note: a desert is a wilderness

indicators.note: returns means the words for no and one are read back to front

parts.note: NO plus I, the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Nobody comes back from the wild, and for a soldier that may mean a court martial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returns' turns NO I into ION. The definition is a hint at what follows the crime rather than a synonym, hence 'may'.
explanation.definitionFit: A soldier who abandons their post commits desertion, a military offence tried by court martial.

clue.text: Condition of the country

definitions.meaning: a ... is a condition, as in a ... of repair

explanation.surface: A report on how the nation is faring.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both the condition something is in and a sovereign nation.

clue.text: Distributors of magazine items

parts.note: sounds like newsagents handing out articles, but a magazine is also an ammunition store, and its items are shells

explanation.surface: A description of the people who deliver periodicals.
explanation.definitionFit: Big guns deliver shells drawn from an ammunition magazine, so they distribute its contents.

clue.text: Signs of distress about rents

explanation.surface: Someone crying over what they pay to the landlord.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rents' looks like payments to a landlord, but is the noun for rips.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both drops shed when crying and rips in fabric, the two senses differing in pronunciation.

clue.text: Writer's reflection in Kent river

definitions.note: the 's stands for is: the writer is the reflection

indicators.note: reflection means what follows is seen mirrored, back to front

parts.note: Kent is in the South East of England, abbreviated SE
the Tay is a Scottish river

explanation.surface: An author's image seen mirrored in a river in Kent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reflection' turns SETAY round. Dornford Yates was an English novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: Dornford Yates was the pen name of an English author of thrillers and comic novels, so he is a writer.

clue.text: Family put into the street with no money

indicators.note: put into means the family word goes inside the street abbreviation

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for street
kin means family or relatives

explanation.surface: A family evicted onto the street without a penny.
explanation.walkthrough: SKINT is British slang for broke.
explanation.definitionFit: Skint is informal British slang for penniless, having no money at all.

clue.text: See Salvation Army gets drink

parts.note: rum is an alcoholic drink

explanation.surface: Watch the Salvation Army get a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' looks like a verb but is a bishop's diocese; Sarum is the old name for Salisbury.
explanation.definitionFit: Sarum is the traditional name of the diocese of Salisbury, so it is a bishop's see.

clue.text: Figure, one short in the arms

definitions.note: in coats of arms, that is in heraldry

indicators.note: one short means the shape is missing one of its letters

parts.note: a triangle is a geometric figure
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A shape that falls one short when held in someone's arms.
explanation.walkthrough: The trangle is a heraldic band, a narrow diminutive of the fess; 'arms' means a coat of arms, not limbs or weapons.
explanation.definitionFit: A trangle is a narrow horizontal bar used on heraldic shields, so it is something found on coats of arms.

clue.text: Fear that's for nothing but a dog

indicators.note: for means one piece is swapped in place of another

parts.note: terror is extreme fear
O looks like zero, nothing
that's means that is, abbreviated i.e.

explanation.surface: Fear is pointless, as it's only a dog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' swaps IE in place of the O in TERROR.
explanation.definitionFit: A terrier is a small, lively breed of dog originally bred for hunting vermin.

clue.text: Shit stablemen swept up for the great and the good

indicators.note: swept up means the words are gathered together and rearranged

explanation.surface: Muck cleared from the stables by grooms for the benefit of the elite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swept up' rearranges SHIT STABLEMEN; the surface is a groom's chore.
explanation.definitionFit: The Establishment is the ruling elite of a society, the influential people known as the great and the good.
